route: lane-reuse: lane re-use with the correct rise accounting, aiming at a superlinear one-player all-switches family
headline: The reopening premise is FALSE and now provably so: the impedance denominator amplifies the GAP, not the RISE. New law lane:rise-bound (a resting Max vertex's rise is at most the largest rise among the vertices its later action reads) proves it, and yields lane:peak-source (the peak of val_{t'}-val_t over ANY interval sits on S_t, sharper than thm:peak-law) and lane:autonomy (an autonomous module's own switched sets are pairwise distinct, so a self-contained lane can never oscillate). lane:exit-chain closes the single-driver two-phase lane by a delay+reach<=k+1 budget. No superlinear family; instead the linear state of the art is improved from fs14:lane-def's N=Theta(k log k) to RC(k): N=k+2, a=0, L=N-2, which is optimal at a=0.

results.name: lane:rise-bound
results.statement: Let G be a stopping SSG, C = Vmax u Vmin, and for u in C, a in {0,1} let (p^{u,a}, q^{u,a}) be the first-passage law of that action onto C u {t1} (a datum of the GRAPH, strategy-independent, since only average vertices lie strictly between controlled vertices). Let sigma, sigma' be Max strategies with val_{sigma'} >= val_sigma pointwise and let u in Vmax be NOT strictly switchable at sigma. Put b := sigma'(u) and W(u,b) := {w in C\{u} : p^{u,b}_w > 0}. Then val_{sigma'}(u) - val_sigma(u) <= max_{w in W(u,b)} ( val_{sigma'}(w) - val_sigma(w) ), the max over the empty set being 0.
results.argument: val_sigma is a fixed point of T_sigma, hence the mean of its successors at every average vertex, so val_tau(u) = sum_w p^{u,tau(u)}_w val_tau(w) + q^{u,tau(u)}. 'At rest' gives, for BOTH actions and in particular for b, p_u x(u) + sum_{w!=u} p_w x(w) + q <= x(u) where x = val_sigma. Since sigma'(u) = b, y(u) = p_u y(u) + sum_{w!=u} p_w y(w) + q with y = val_{sigma'}. Subtracting and using sum_{w!=u} p_w <= 1 - p_u - q <= 1 - p_u gives (1-p_u)(y(u)-x(u)) <= sum_{w!=u} p_w Delta_w <= (1-p_u) M. Finally p_u < 1, since p_u = 1 would make {u} plus the average vertices on those paths a trap, contradicting stopping (lem:trapchar).
results.verification: Exact rational arithmetic. 74232 instances (game, sigma, sigma', u) over random one-player harmonic normal forms with m <= 6 (t_rise.py); a further 10933 at the SSG level over random stopping games with 3-8 non-sinks, BOTH players present, with the first-passage laws recomputed from the graph (t_laws.py). No violation. Transcript VERIFY.log.

results.name: lane:impedance-cancels
results.statement: Let G be stopping, sigma_0..sigma_L an all-switches run, u in Vmax at rest at sigma_t, and suppose u in S_{t'} for some t' >= t, switching to action b with return mass h = p^{u,b}_u = h(b -> u) (so thm:impedance writes the rise in that round as (val_{sigma_{t'}}(b) - val_{sigma_{t'}}(a))/(1-h)). Then val_{sigma_{t'+1}}(u) - val_{sigma_t}(u) <= max_{w in W(u,b)} ( val_{sigma_{t'+1}}(w) - val_{sigma_t}(w) ). So a delayed switch can gain far more than the GAP that triggered it, and never more than the RISE of its trigger.
results.argument: lane:rise-bound with sigma = sigma_t, sigma' = sigma_{t'+1}; sigma_{t'+1}(u) = b and val_{sigma_{t'+1}} >= val_{sigma_t} by lem:switch. The route was opened on the premise that 'the escape denominator 1-h can be 2^{-Theta(N)}, so a delayed switch CAN gain far more than its trigger did'. Written out: before the switch val(b) = h val(u) + (1-h) l, so the gap is (1-h)(l - val(u)) while the rise is l - val(u) (allswlower:cor-selfread) -- the ratio 1/(1-h) is indeed unbounded; but l - val(u) is itself bounded by the largest rise among the vertices b reads, over the whole waiting period. The premise is therefore false as stated and true only in the weaker form 'more than the gap'.
results.verification: Implied by lane:rise-bound (verified as above); additionally exercised by every all-switches run in t_rise.py / t_laws.py.

results.name: lane:peak-source
results.statement: Let G be stopping and sigma_0..sigma_L an all-switches run. For all 0 <= t < t' <= L, max_{v in V} (val_{sigma_{t'}}(v) - val_{sigma_t}(v)) = max_{v in S_t} (val_{sigma_{t'}}(v) - val_{sigma_t}(v)). Taking t=0, t'=L: the whole improvement of the run is realised at a vertex strictly switchable at the very first round.
results.argument: Put Delta = val_{sigma_{t'}} - val_{sigma_t} >= 0 (lem:switch) and A = C \ S_t. The computation in lane:rise-bound gives, for u in A n Vmax with b = sigma_{t'}(u), Delta_u <= sum_{w != u} tilde-p_w Delta_w with tilde-p_w = p^{u,b}_w/(1-p^{u,b}_u), row sums <= 1; the SAME inequality holds at u in Vmin with b the action of a Min best response to sigma_t, since val_{sigma_{t'}}(u) is a minimum over actions hence at most the value of that one, while val_{sigma_t}(u) equals it. Collecting rows, Delta|_A <= Q Delta|_A + R Delta|_{S_t} with [Q R] substochastic; tilde-P is the jump chain of the transient P (I - tilde-P = (I-D)^{-1}(I-P)), hence transient, hence so is Q; so Delta|_A <= (I-Q)^{-1} R Delta|_{S_t} and (I-Q)^{-1} R 1 <= 1 (probabilities of ever leaving A into S_t). Averages and sinks add nothing.
results.verification: Exact. All pairs t < t' of all-switches runs from EVERY start: 5572 pairs on one-player normal forms (t_rise.py) and 283 on random two-player stopping games (t_laws.py). No violation. This is strictly sharper than thm:peak-law in the direction that matters: the peak of any interval is pinned to the set switched at the START of the interval, for all later t' at once.

results.name: lane:autonomy + lane:modules
results.statement: Call U subset of Vmax AUTONOMOUS in a one-player SSG if W(u,a) is contained in U for every u in U and both a. Then along any all-switches run, t -> S_t n U is exactly the all-switches switch sequence of the sub-SSG G|_U from sigma_0|_U, padded with the empty set. Hence (a) once S_t n U is empty it is empty for ever; (b) the nonempty sets among S_t n U are PAIRWISE DISTINCT; (c) #{t : S_t n U nonempty} <= h*(|U|), and <= h*_HK(|U|) if G|_U is nondegenerate. Corollary (lane:modules): if Vmax partitions into autonomous modules then L = max_i L_i, so placing gadgets side by side never lengthens a run; a gadget to be run twice must read a vertex outside itself.
results.argument: By the first-passage identity and autonomy, val_sigma|_U solves the linear system of G|_U determined by sigma|_U alone, so val_sigma|_U = val^{G|_U}_{sigma|_U}; hence S_sigma n U depends only on sigma|_U and equals S^{G|_U}_{sigma|_U}. The projection of the run is therefore the all-switches run of G|_U, which stops when its switch set empties and then stays put -- (a). (b) is cor:law-u applied to G|_U; (c) is cor:ceiling-general with prop:oneplayer-lp. G|_U is stopping because a trap of G|_U is a trap of G.
results.verification: Exact: 610 projected switch sequences over all autonomous U with |U| <= 4, on random stopping games with both players (t_laws.py). No violation. This is the MODULE form of allswlower:lem-isolated(ii): a self-contained lane cannot repeat ANY of its own switch patterns, so no external stimulation can make it oscillate, and cor:law-u bites inside the module even when the ambient switched sets are all distinct.

results.name: lane:exit-chain + lane:budget
results.statement: Let G be one-player stopping, l_1..l_n, d in Vmax distinct, with one action b_i of l_i having W(l_i,b_i) contained in {l_{i-1}} (l_0 := d) and BOTH actions of d having read set inside {l_1..l_j}. If at some round t of an improving run sigma_t(l_i) = b_i for all i <= j and d is not strictly switchable, then at every later round at which all l_i (i<=j) are again at b_i we have sigma_{t'}(d) = sigma_t(d) and val unchanged on {d, l_1..l_j}; so as soon as one of these has strictly raised its value, that configuration never occurs again. Consequently in the two-phase lane the driver cannot fire before round k-j+1 (val(l_j) has not moved before then) and the exit wave can never reach l_j, so delay + reach <= k+1 whatever j: the two-phase lane runs at most k+O(1) rounds.
results.argument: W := {d, l_1..l_j} with pi_a := (d -> a, l_i -> b_i) is a CLOSED CONFIGURATION in the sense of prop:closed-now-or-never for each of d's two actions a (everything reachable from pi_a(W) avoiding W is average or a sink). Take a = the action d does NOT take at sigma_t; then W_t = {d}, nonempty and disjoint from S_{sigma_t}, so prop:closed-now-or-never(b) forbids sigma_{t'}|_W = pi_a for ever. Hence the only way all l_i can be at b_i again is with d unchanged, i.e. sigma_{t'}|_W = sigma_t|_W, and W is closed for that too, so the values on W are the same lambda_W.
results.verification: Exact scan over the two-phase lane family (mass alpha, per-vertex rewards, both read points, all parameters dyadic with denominator 256, k=5, |Vmax|=7): longest run found 7 rounds = |Vmax| (t_lane2.py). Replacing the single driver by turnaround vertices reading MIXTURES of the whole lane removes the closed set and therefore this obstruction; an exact scan of that family (rl.py, k <= 5) also found nothing longer than |Vmax|.

results.name: lane:three + lane:linear (RC, ALH, CL)
results.statement: RC(k): Vmax = v_1..v_k, NO average vertex, v_i -> (v_{i+1}, t0) for i<k, v_k -> (t1, t0). ALH(k): Vmax = p_1..p_k, one average vertex h -> (t1,t0), p_i -> (p_{i+1}, h), p_{k+1} := t1. CL(k): Vmax = l_1..l_k, Vavg = g_1..g_k, l_i -> (l_{i+1}, g_i) with l_{k+1} := t1, g_i -> (l_{i-1}, t0), g_1 -> (t1, t0). All three are one-player and stopping and, from the start taking the second listed action everywhere, the all-switches run switches exactly ONE vertex per round in the order k, k-1, ..., 1, halting at w* = 1 on Vmax. Hence RC(k): N = k+2, a = 0, L = N-2; ALH(k): N = k+3, a = 1, L = N-3; CL(k): N = 2k+2, a = k, L = (N-2)/2. RC and ALH have C(k,2) tied incidences along the run, CL none; all three are degenerate as cube orientations (CL's cube ties are 0,2,12,46,144 for k=2..6), so thm:flat-resolution and not prop:allsw-auso applies, and the Holt-Klee ceiling does not bind them.
results.argument: RC: at the all-t0 strategy every val(v_i)=0; for i<k the other option is val(v_{i+1})=0, a TIE (all-switches keeps ties), while v_k sees 1>0. Inductively after r rounds v_{k-r+1}..v_k have value 1 and exactly v_{k-r} switches; a vertex's value is 1 after switching so it never switches again. ALH: identical with 0 replaced by 1/2 = val(h). CL: at the all-exit strategy val(g_1)=1/2 and val(g_i)=val(l_{i-1})/2, so val(l_i)=2^{-i}, strictly decreasing, so no premature switch; l_k sees 1>2^{-k}; l_i switching to continue only lowers val(g_{i+1}) to 1/2 < 1 so nothing switches back. Stopping by lem:trapchar (RC's Max subgraph is acyclic; in ALH and CL every average vertex has t0 as a successor).
results.verification: Exact, from the GRAPH, with the harness's independent all-switches loop (rc.py, alh.py, chainlane.py). RC verified for k = 2,3,4,5,8,12,20,50,100; ALH for k up to 80; CL for k up to 30; the optimum w* = 1 checked by brute force over all strategies for the small k. Degeneracy and Holt-Klee audit in t_hk.py. These improve fs14:lane-def, which needs N = Theta(k log k) for the same run length k (its N = 13,24,43,64,124 at k=3,5,8,12,20 reproduced here).

results.name: lane:grid + lane:rc-optimal
results.statement: Let G be a stopping SSG with m = |Vmax|, a = |Vavg|, and let D(a) = |{p/q in [0,1] : 1 <= q <= 2^a}| be the number of points of the grid of lem:denominator-sharp. Then every all-switches run satisfies L <= sum_{v in Vmax} n_v <= m (D(a) - 1), where n_v is the number of rounds at which v switches. In particular L <= m when a = 0 and L <= 2m when a = 1. Hence RC(k) is OPTIMAL among one-player stopping SSGs with no average vertex (L <= |Vmax| = N-2, attained), and any one-player family with L > N-2 must have a >= 1 and must switch some vertex more than once.
results.argument: Each round switches a nonempty set, so L <= sum_v n_v. If v switches at rounds t_1 < ... < t_{n_v}, lem:switch makes val(v) strictly larger after each of them and non-decreasing in between, so v takes at least n_v + 1 distinct values along the run, all on the grid of lem:denominator-sharp.
results.verification: Exact search with a and m held fixed (fixeda.py): at a=0 the bound L = m is attained for m = 3,4,5,6 (and the search found 6 at m=7,8, below the bound but RC attains it); at a=1 the search returned L = m exactly for m = 3..7 and at a=2 L = m for m = 3..6 -- always far below the grid bound m 2^a, so the extra randomness bought nothing at these sizes.

results.name: lane:tree + lane:tree-lag (binarisation)
results.statement: A state with r >= 2 actions is replaced by a rooted binary tree of r-1 fresh Max vertices whose r leaf edges carry the actions' first-passage laws; if the r action values do not change during d = ceil(log2 r) consecutive rounds of an all-switches run, the root then selects a leaf of maximal value and has value max_i val(A_i). Cost: r-1 Max vertices, no average vertices. The lag is real: an explicit 15-vertex one-player stopping SSG (Lane(3) with exits 7/8, 3/4, 5/8, plus u = max(l_1,l_2), p = max(u,l_3)) has an all-switches run of 3 rounds in which, at round 1, the best leaf is worth 1 while the root p is worth 7/8.
results.argument: Induction on height: a height-1 vertex compares its two leaves and after one round selects the larger; if every vertex of height <= j selects its subtree maximum after j rounds, a height-(j+1) vertex sees the two subtree maxima from round j and after one more round selects the larger. Ties are kept, harmlessly. The instance is computed exactly and its normal form is re-derived from the realised graph.
results.verification: tree.py, exact: normal form realised as an honest SSG (N=15, 5 Max, 8 average, stopping), first-passage laws re-verified from the graph, and the SSG-level all-switches loop reproduces the run (3 rounds, trace [(2,), (1,4), (0,3)], 2 ties).

results.name: lane:measured / lane:nminus2
results.statement: Longest all-switches runs found for ONE-PLAYER stopping games. (i) Local search over harmonic normal forms (each action reading at most 3 Max vertices, dyadic denominator 32 or 64, objective the bottom-antipodal height over all 2^m starts): m=4 -> 6, m=5 -> 8, m=6 -> 8, m=7 -> 8. The 6 at m=4 is exactly h*_HK(4), the ceiling of prop:oneplayer-lp; the height-8 instance at m=5 is DEGENERATE (2 tied incidences over the cube, none along the run) so not bound by that ceiling, and in its run one Max vertex switches four times and a second switches four times. (ii) Local search at the level of the graph over one-player stopping SSGs with n = N-2 non-sinks and every (|Vmax|,|Vavg|) split: L = 5,6,7,8,8,9 at n = 5..10 -- never more than n = N-2, which RC(n) attains. QUESTION: is L <= N-2 for every one-player stopping SSG?
results.argument: Simulated annealing with exact rational evaluation; the fast evaluator (all 2^m value vectors -> outmap -> bottom-antipodal height) was validated against the direct all-switches loop on 1696 (game, start) pairs. This is a measurement over an engineered search space and proves nothing -- no search in this project has ever found a hard instance that was not first engineered.
results.verification: search1/2/3.py, ssgsearch.py, seeded.py, fixeda.py; inspect.py replays any logged instance, realises it as an honest SSG and re-checks the run with the independent SSG-level loop (done for the m=4 height-6 and m=5 height-8 instances: N = 54 and 55, normal form verified from the graph, SSG run identical).

gap: A one-player stopping SSG family on N = k^{O(1)} vertices whose all-switches run has length omega(N) is not constructed, and the single architecture the route's own theorems leave open is this: a lane l_1,...,l_k whose two turnaround vertices B (at the foot of the exit chain) and T (at the head of the continue chain) each read a MIXTURE of ALL of l_1,...,l_k, so that no proper subset of Vmax is a closed configuration and prop:closed-now-or-never/lane:exit-chain are vacuous, while lane:autonomy forces the lane's own switch pattern to vary from epoch to epoch, which it can do only if the ambient (B,T) state differs -- exact scans of this family were run only for k <= 5 and found nothing longer than |Vmax|. Second, separate gap (task 4): is there a choice of binary selection trees and delay chains for Fearnley's MDP, of total size n^{O(1)}, such that the all-switches run of the resulting two-action instance reproduces the appeal ordering at every bit state in every round -- equivalently, such that for every i and every round the root of b_i's tree selects the same action that b_i selects in the source instance, up to a fixed per-state lag?
next_steps:
1. The one architecture left open (mixture-driven turnarounds) needs a k >= 6 scan, which needs a better evaluator than annealing over 2^m starts: evaluate only from the designed all-D start and search the (mass, reward) parameters by exact bisection on the crossing conditions rather than by random moves. Two lanes of COPRIME lengths, weakly cross-coupled, are the natural candidate: lane:autonomy forbids either lane to repeat a switch pattern on its own, but the union's sets stay distinct if the two waves are out of phase, and the arithmetic (the loop gain is < 1, so the per-epoch rises shrink geometrically and j epochs need only Theta(j) bits, i.e. a = Theta(j) average vertices) does NOT forbid j = Theta(k) epochs and hence L = Theta(k^2). Nothing in this round refutes that; nothing in this round realises it either.
2. Settle lane:nminus2 (is L <= N-2 for every one-player stopping SSG?). At a = 0 it is a theorem (lane:grid); at a = 1 the grid bound is 2m and the measured maximum is m, so the first thing to decide is whether L = 2m is realisable at a = 1 -- a small, self-contained question that would already give L = 2N - 6, twice RC.
3. The ceiling question the measurements point at: how fast does h*_HK(m) grow? h*_HK = 1,2,4,6,11 for m <= 5 (the value 11 is measured and unverified), against the search's realisable 6,8,8,8 at m = 4,5,6,7. If h*_HK is superpolynomial the one-player half of the pivot is a pure realisability question; if it is linear, prop:oneplayer-lp settles the nondegenerate one-player half negatively and every superlinear one-player family must be degenerate (as RC, ALH and CL already are). Verifying h*_HK(5) = 11 and then attempting a one-player realisation of a height-11 Holt-Klee AUSO of the 5-cube is the decisive small computation.
4. lane:peak-source should be checked against the wedge and CC families: it pins the peak of every interval to S_t, so it may give an unconditional lower bound on how early a value-distinguishing pair must separate.

\subsection{What a resting vertex can gain}
\label{sec:lane}

Throughout this subsection $G$ is a stopping SSG, $C:=\Vmax\cup\Vmin$, and for
$u\in C$ and $a\in\{0,1\}$ we write $(p^{u,a},q^{u,a})$ for the \emph{first
passage law} of the $a$-th action of $u$ onto $C\cup\{t_1\}$: $p^{u,a}_w$ is the
probability that the token, having left $u$ by that edge, next meets a
controlled vertex at $w$, and $q^{u,a}$ the probability that it reaches $t_1$
before any controlled vertex. Only average vertices lie strictly between two
controlled vertices, so $(p^{u,a},q^{u,a})$ is a datum of the \emph{graph},
independent of both strategies, and every value vector satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{lane:eq-fp}
  \val_\sigma(u)\;=\;\sum_{w\in C}p^{u,\sigma(u)}_w\val_\sigma(w)+q^{u,\sigma(u)}
  \qquad(u\in\Vmax),
\end{equation}
because $\val_\sigma$ is a fixed point of $T_\sigma$ and is therefore the mean of
its successors at every average vertex. The same identity holds at $u\in\Vmin$
with $\sigma(u)$ replaced by any Min best response to $\sigma$. Write
$W(u,a):=\{w\in C\setminus\{u\}:p^{u,a}_w>0\}$, the \emph{read set} of the
action, and call $u\in\Vmax$ \emph{at rest} at $\sigma$ if $u\notin S_\sigma$.

\begin{lemma}[Rise bound]\label{lane:rise-bound}
Let $G$ be stopping, let $\sigma,\sigma'$ be Max strategies with
$\val_{\sigma'}\ge\val_\sigma$ pointwise, and let $u\in\Vmax$ be at rest at
$\sigma$. Put $b:=\sigma'(u)$. Then
\[
  \val_{\sigma'}(u)-\val_\sigma(u)\;\le\;
  \max_{w\in W(u,b)}\bigl(\val_{\sigma'}(w)-\val_\sigma(w)\bigr),
\]
the maximum over the empty set being $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $x:=\val_\sigma$, $y:=\val_{\sigma'}$, $\Delta_w:=y(w)-x(w)\ge0$,
$M:=\max_{w\in W(u,b)}\Delta_w\ge0$, $p:=p^{u,b}$, $q:=q^{u,b}$. Being at rest
means that \emph{both} actions of $u$ have value at most $x(u)$ under $x$; for
the action $b$ this reads, by \eqref{lane:eq-fp} applied to a strategy taking
$b$ at $u$,
\[
  p_u\,x(u)+\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\,x(w)+q\;\le\;x(u).
\]
Since $\sigma'(u)=b$, \eqref{lane:eq-fp} gives
$y(u)=p_uy(u)+\sum_{w\ne u}p_wy(w)+q$. Subtracting, and using
$\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\le 1-p_u$,
\[
  (1-p_u)\bigl(y(u)-x(u)\bigr)\;\le\;\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\Delta_w\;\le\;(1-p_u)M .
\]
Finally $p_u<1$: if $p_u=1$ the action $b$ would return to $u$ with probability
one, so $\{u\}$ together with the average vertices on those paths would be a
trap, contradicting stopping (\Cref{lem:trapchar}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No overtaking]\label{lane:no-overtake}
Let $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ be a run of improving switches on a stopping SSG,
$u\in\Vmax$, and let $b$ be an action of $u$ with $W(u,b)=\{w\}$ a single
controlled vertex. If $u\notin S_{\sigma_t}$ and $\sigma_{t'}(u)=b$ for some
$t'>t$, then
\[
  \val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)-\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(w)\;\le\;
  \val_{\sigma_t}(u)-\val_{\sigma_t}(w).
\]
In particular, if $\val_{\sigma_t}(u)\le\val_{\sigma_t}(w)$ then
$\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)\le\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(w)$ for every such $t'$: a vertex
that is once at rest never overtakes the single vertex its action reads.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The peak of an interval sits on $S_t$]\label{lane:peak-source}
Let $G$ be stopping and $\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run. For all
$0\le t<t'\le L$,
\[
  \max_{v\in V}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(v)-\val_{\sigma_t}(v)\bigr)
  \;=\;\max_{v\in S_t}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(v)-\val_{\sigma_t}(v)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
``$\ge$'' is trivial. Put $\Delta:=\val_{\sigma_{t'}}-\val_{\sigma_t}\ge0$
(\Cref{lem:switch}) and $A:=C\setminus S_t$. The computation in the proof of
\Cref{lane:rise-bound} gives, for every $u\in A\cap\Vmax$ with
$b=\sigma_{t'}(u)$,
\[
  \Delta_u\;\le\;\sum_{w\ne u}\tilde p_w\Delta_w,\qquad
  \tilde p_w:=\frac{p^{u,b}_w}{1-p^{u,b}_u},\qquad \sum_{w\ne u}\tilde p_w\le1 ,
\]
and the same inequality holds at $u\in\Vmin$ with $b$ the action of a Min best
response to $\sigma_t$, because there $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)$ is a minimum over
actions, hence at most the value of that particular one, while
$\val_{\sigma_t}(u)$ equals it. Collecting these rows, $\Delta|_A\le
Q\,\Delta|_A+R\,\Delta|_{S_t}$ with $[Q\ R]$ substochastic. The matrix
$\tilde P$ is the jump chain of the transient substochastic $P$ obtained by
deleting self-loops and renormalising, and $I-\tilde P=(I-D)^{-1}(I-P)$ with
$D=\operatorname{diag}(p_{uu})$, so $\tilde P$ is transient too and so is its
submatrix $Q$. Hence $\Delta|_A\le(I-Q)^{-1}R\,\Delta|_{S_t}$, and
$(I-Q)^{-1}R\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$ (it is the vector of probabilities of ever
leaving $A$ into $S_t$). Therefore $\max_A\Delta\le\max_{S_t}\Delta$. Values at
average vertices are means of values at $C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$ and the sinks have
$\Delta=0$, so the maximum over $V$ is the maximum over $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:peak-vs-peak-law}
\Cref{lane:peak-source} is sharper than \Cref{thm:peak-law} in the direction
that matters for lower-bound constructions: the peak of $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}-
\val_{\sigma_t}$ lies on the set switched \emph{at the beginning} of the
interval, for every later $t'$ at once, and $|S_t|\le|\Vmax|$. Taking $t=0$ and
$t'=L$: the whole improvement of the run is realised at a vertex that is
strictly switchable at the very first round.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Verification]\label{lane:verify-laws}
All three statements were verified in exact rational arithmetic.
\Cref{lane:rise-bound}: $74\,232$ instances $(\text{game},\sigma,\sigma',u)$ on
random one-player normal forms with $m\le6$, and a further $10\,933$ at the SSG
level on random stopping games with $3$--$8$ non-sinks, both players present
(so both the $\Vmax$ and the $\Vmin$ rows of the proof are exercised); no
violation. \Cref{lane:peak-source}: all pairs $t<t'$ of all-switches runs from
every start, $5\,572$ pairs on one-player normal forms and $283$ on random
two-player stopping games; no violation. \Cref{lane:autonomy} below: $610$
projected switch sequences over all autonomous $U$ with $|U|\le4$; no
violation. Files \texttt{t\_rise.py}, \texttt{t\_laws.py}; transcript
\texttt{VERIFY.log}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Autonomy: a self-contained module is never re-run}

\begin{definition}[Autonomous module]\label{lane:autonomous}
$U\subseteq\Vmax$ is \emph{autonomous} in a one-player SSG $G$ if
$W(u,a)\subseteq U$ for every $u\in U$ and both $a$ --- equivalently, every
path leaving a vertex of $U$ meets a sink or a vertex of $U$ before any other
Max vertex. Then $G|_U$, the sub-SSG induced on $U$ together with the average
vertices met on those paths, is a stopping SSG in its own right (its vertices
have the same out-edges as in $G$, and a trap of $G|_U$ would be a trap of
$G$).
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Autonomy law]\label{lane:autonomy}
Let $G$ be a one-player stopping SSG, $U$ autonomous, and
$\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run with switch sets $S_0,\dots,S_{L-1}$.
Then $t\mapsto S_t\cap U$ is the switch sequence of the all-switches run of the
stopping game $G|_U$ from $\sigma_0|_U$, padded with $\emptyset$; in particular
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item once $S_t\cap U=\emptyset$, $S_{t'}\cap U=\emptyset$ for all $t'\ge t$;
\item the nonempty sets among $S_0\cap U,\dots,S_{L-1}\cap U$ are pairwise
      distinct;
\item $\#\{t:S_t\cap U\ne\emptyset\}\le h^\ast(|U|)$, and
      $\le h^\ast_{HK}(|U|)$ if moreover $G|_U$ is nondegenerate.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{lane:eq-fp} and autonomy the restriction $\val_\sigma|_U$ solves the
linear system of $G|_U$ determined by $\sigma|_U$ alone, so
$\val_\sigma|_U=\val_{\sigma|_U}^{G|_U}$. Hence $S_\sigma\cap U$
depends only on $\sigma|_U$ and equals $S^{G|_U}_{\sigma|_U}$. Therefore the
projection of the run is exactly the all-switches run of $G|_U$, which stops
when its switch set is empty --- and then stays put, giving (a). (b) is
\Cref{cor:law-u} applied to $G|_U$, and (c) is \Cref{cor:ceiling-general}
together with \Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Modules do not add up]\label{lane:modules}
If $\Vmax=U_1\uplus\dots\uplus U_r$ with every $U_i$ autonomous, then the
all-switches run of $G$ has length $\max_i L_i$, where $L_i$ is the length of
the run of $G|_{U_i}$ from $\sigma_0|_{U_i}$. Placing gadgets side by side
therefore never lengthens a run; a gadget that is to be run twice must have an
action reading a vertex outside itself.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:autonomy-vs-isolated}
\Cref{lane:autonomy} is the module form of \Cref{allswlower:lem-isolated}(ii),
which is its case ``$U$ is switched alone in one round''. What it adds is that
the impossibility of a reset is not a property of a single quiet round: an
autonomous module can never repeat \emph{any} of its own switch patterns, so
no amount of external stimulation can make a self-contained lane oscillate,
and \Cref{cor:law-u} bites inside the module even when the ambient switched
sets are all distinct.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The impedance denominator buys nothing}

\Cref{thm:impedance} says that the rise produced by switching $u$ is
$(f(b)-f(a))/(1-h(b\!\to\!u))$, and $1-h$ can be $2^{-\Theta(N)}$; the natural
hope --- and the reason this route was opened --- is that a switch delayed long
enough can therefore gain far more than the event that triggered it. It cannot.

\begin{proposition}[Amplification cancels]\label{lane:impedance-cancels}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG, $\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run,
$u\in\Vmax$ at rest at $\sigma_t$, and suppose $u\in S_{t'}$ for some $t'\ge t$
with $b:=\bar\sigma_{t'}(u)$ the action it switches to. Let
$h:=p^{u,b}_u=h(b\!\to\!u)$, so that \Cref{thm:impedance} writes the rise at
$u$ in that round as $\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(b)-\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(a)\bigr)/(1-h)$.
Then
\[
  \val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}(u)-\val_{\sigma_t}(u)\;\le\;
  \max_{w\in W(u,b)}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}(w)-\val_{\sigma_t}(w)\bigr).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\Cref{lane:rise-bound} with $\sigma=\sigma_t$, $\sigma'=\sigma_{t'+1}$; note
$\sigma_{t'+1}(u)=b$ and $\val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}\ge\val_{\sigma_t}$ by
\Cref{lem:switch}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The rise accounting]\label{lane:accounting}
The two statements are consistent and say different things. The \emph{gap}
$\val(b)-\val(a)$ that makes $u$ switchable is indeed damped by the loop: if
$b$ returns to $u$ with probability $h$, then before the switch
$\val(b)=h\val(u)+(1-h)\ell$ where $\ell$ is the value of $b$ conditioned on
not returning, so the gap is $(1-h)(\ell-\val(u))$, while the rise is
$\ell-\val(u)$ --- this is \Cref{allswlower:cor-selfread}, and the ratio
$1/(1-h)$ is unbounded. What \Cref{lane:impedance-cancels} adds is that
$\ell-\val(u)$ itself is bounded by the largest rise, over the whole waiting
period, among the vertices $b$ reads. So a delayed switch may gain far more
than the \emph{gap} that triggered it, and never more than the \emph{rise} of
its trigger. The premise on which this route was opened is therefore false in
the form in which it was stated, and true only in the weaker form ``more than
the gap''.

Reconciliation with \Cref{cor:no-return} for a vertex switched twice. Suppose
$u\in S_{t}$ and $u\in S_{t''}$ with $\sigma_{t''+1}(u)=\sigma_t(u)$, i.e.\ $u$
returns to an old action. By \Cref{lem:switch} $\val(u)$ rises strictly at each
of the two switches, so the second switch does have a rise; by
\Cref{cor:no-return} applied to $t<t''+1$ the set $S_t$ must contain a vertex
at which $\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_{t''+1}$ differ, and that vertex is not $u$, so
$S_t\ne\{u\}$ --- a vertex switched \emph{alone} never switches again
(\Cref{allswlower:lem-isolated}(i)). The size of the second rise is then
governed by \Cref{lane:rise-bound} applied from any round in $(t,t'')$ at which
$u$ was at rest: it is at most the largest rise, over that interval, of the
vertices the restored action reads. Nothing in the two-switch pattern is
paid for by the escape denominator.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[An exit chain never passes its driver's read point]\label{lane:exit-chain}
Let $G$ be a one-player stopping SSG and let $l_1,\dots,l_n,d\in\Vmax$ be
distinct. Suppose that for each $i$ one action $b_i$ of $l_i$ has
$W(l_i,b_i)\subseteq\{l_{i-1}\}$, where $l_0:=d$, and that both actions of $d$
have $W(d,\cdot)\subseteq\{l_1,\dots,l_j\}$ for some $j\le n$. Let
$\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ be a run of improving switches and suppose that at
some round $t$
\[
  \sigma_t(l_i)=b_i\ (1\le i\le j)\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\notin S_{\sigma_t}.
\]
Then for every $t'>t$ at which $\sigma_{t'}(l_i)=b_i$ for all $i\le j$ we have
$\sigma_{t'}(d)=\sigma_t(d)$ and $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}=\val_{\sigma_t}$ on
$\{d,l_1,\dots,l_j\}$. Consequently, as soon as one of
$d,l_1,\dots,l_j$ has strictly raised its value since round $t$, the
configuration $(\sigma(l_1),\dots,\sigma(l_j))=(b_1,\dots,b_j)$ never occurs
again.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $W:=\{d,l_1,\dots,l_j\}$ and, for each action $a$ of $d$,
$\pi_a:=(d\mapsto a,\ l_i\mapsto b_i)$. Every vertex reachable from $\pi_a(W)$
without meeting $W$ again is an average vertex or a sink, so $(W,\pi_a)$ is a
closed configuration in the sense of \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never}. Let $a$
be the action of $d$ \emph{not} taken at $\sigma_t$. Then
$W_t=\{v\in W:\sigma_t(v)\ne\pi_a(v)\}=\{d\}$ is nonempty and meets
$S_{\sigma_t}$ not at all, so \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never}(b) gives
$\sigma_{t'}|_W\ne\pi_a$ for every $t'\ge t$. Hence if all $l_i$, $i\le j$,
are at $b_i$ at $\sigma_{t'}$, then $\sigma_{t'}(d)=\sigma_t(d)$, i.e.\
$\sigma_{t'}|_W=\sigma_t|_W$, and since $W$ is closed for that configuration
too, the values on $W$ are the same vector $\lambda_W$ at both rounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The delay/reach budget of a two-phase lane]\label{lane:budget}
This is exactly what stops the construction the route set out to build. Take
the lane $l_i\to(l_{i+1},\ \text{exit}_i)$ with $\text{exit}_i$ reading
$l_{i-1}$ and $l_0=d$ a driver whose idle action is a constant and whose other
action reads $l_j$. Then:
\emph{(i)} the driver cannot fire before the first (``continue'') wave has
reached $l_j$, i.e.\ before round $k-j+1$, because until then $\val(l_j)$ has
not moved; and
\emph{(ii)} by \Cref{lane:exit-chain} the second (``exit'') wave, which
travels $l_1,l_2,\dots$, can never reach $l_j$, so it makes at most $j-1$
switches.
Delay plus reach is therefore at most $k+1$, whatever $j$: the two-phase lane
has an all-switches run of at most $k+O(1)$ rounds, i.e.\ no better than the
plain lane it was built from. This was confirmed by an exact scan over the
family (masses, rewards, both read points, all parameters dyadic with
denominator $256$): the longest run found at $k=5$, $|\Vmax|=7$, is $7$ rounds
(\texttt{t\_lane2.py}). Replacing the single driver by drivers reading
mixtures of the whole lane removes the closed set --- and therefore removes
this obstruction --- but the same scan over that family
(\texttt{rl.py}, $k\le5$) also found nothing longer than $|\Vmax|$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{How cheap a linear lane is, and what the value grid allows}

The lane of \Cref{fs14:lane-def} spends $\Theta(\log k)$ average vertices per
Max vertex to make its $k$ exit values distinct. None of that is needed.

\begin{definition}[Three linear lanes]\label{lane:three}
For $k\ge2$:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.6em]
\item $RC(k)$ (\emph{reachability chain}): $\Vmax=\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}$, no average
vertex, $v_i\to(v_{i+1},t_0)$ for $i<k$ and $v_k\to(t_1,t_0)$.
\item $ALH(k)$ (\emph{all-half chain}): $\Vmax=\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$, one average
vertex $h\to(t_1,t_0)$, and $p_i\to(p_{i+1},h)$ with $p_{k+1}:=t_1$.
\item $CL(k)$ (\emph{damped lane}): $\Vmax=\{l_1,\dots,l_k\}$,
$\Vavg=\{g_1,\dots,g_k\}$, $l_i\to(l_{i+1},g_i)$ with $l_{k+1}:=t_1$,
$g_i\to(l_{i-1},t_0)$ and $g_1\to(t_1,t_0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{lane:linear}
All three are one-player and stopping, and from the start that takes the second
listed action everywhere the all-switches run switches exactly one vertex per
round, in the order $k,k-1,\dots,1$, and halts at the optimum $w^\ast\equiv1$
on $\Vmax$. Hence
\[
  RC(k):\ N=k+2,\ a=0,\ L=N-2;\qquad
  ALH(k):\ N=k+3,\ a=1,\ L=N-3;\qquad
  CL(k):\ N=2k+2,\ a=k,\ L=\tfrac{N-2}2 .
\]
$RC$ and $ALH$ have $\binom k2$ tied incidences along the run, $CL$ has none;
all three are nevertheless degenerate as orientations of the $k$-cube, the tied
incidences of $CL(k)$ over the whole cube being $0,2,12,46,144$ for
$k=2,\dots,6$, so \Cref{thm:flat-resolution} rather than
\Cref{prop:allsw-auso} is what makes their runs bottom-antipodal walks, and
the Holt--Klee ceiling of \Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp} does not apply to them.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Stopping: in $RC$ the graph on $\Vmax$ is acyclic, in $ALH$ and $CL$ every
average vertex has $t_0$ among its successors, so the greatest trap is empty
(\Cref{lem:trapchar}).
$RC$: under the all-$t_0$ strategy every $\val(v_i)=0$; for $i<k$ the other
option is $\val(v_{i+1})=0$, a tie, and all-switches keeps ties, while $v_k$
sees $\val(t_1)=1>0$. Inductively after $r$ rounds $v_{k-r+1},\dots,v_k$ have
value $1$ and the rest $0$, so exactly $v_{k-r}$ switches. Since a vertex's
value is $1$ after it switches, it never switches again.
$ALH$: identical with $0$ replaced by $\tfrac12=\val(h)$ and $1$ by
$\val(t_1)$.
$CL$: under the all-exit strategy $\val(g_1)=\tfrac12$ and
$\val(g_i)=\tfrac12\val(l_{i-1})$, so $\val(l_i)=2^{-i}$; for $i<k$ the other
option is $\val(l_{i+1})=2^{-(i+1)}<2^{-i}$ --- strictly smaller, so no tie and
no switch --- while $l_k$ sees $1>2^{-k}$. After $r$ rounds
$l_{k-r+1},\dots,l_k$ continue with value $1$ and $l_i=2^{-i}$ for $i\le k-r$,
so exactly $l_{k-r}$ switches; and $l_i$ switching to continue only lowers
$\val(g_{i+1})$ to $\tfrac12<1$, so nothing switches back.
The tie counts are the pairs $(i,r)$ with $i<k-r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The value grid bounds the run]\label{lane:grid}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG with $m=|\Vmax|$ and $a=|\Vavg|$, and let
$D(a):=\bigl|\{p/q\in[0,1]:1\le q\le 2^{a}\}\bigr|$ be the number of points of
the grid of \Cref{lem:denominator-sharp}. Then every all-switches run satisfies
\[
  L\;\le\;\sum_{v\in\Vmax}n_v\;\le\;m\,\bigl(D(a)-1\bigr),
\]
where $n_v$ is the number of rounds at which $v$ switches. In particular
$L\le m$ when $a=0$ (grid $\{0,1\}$) and $L\le 2m$ when $a=1$ (grid
$\{0,\tfrac12,1\}$).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each round of the run switches a nonempty set, so $L\le\sum_v n_v$. If $v$
switches at rounds $t_1<\dots<t_{n_v}$ then by \Cref{lem:switch}
$\val_{\sigma_{t_1}}(v)<\val_{\sigma_{t_1+1}}(v)\le\val_{\sigma_{t_2}}(v)<\dots$,
so $v$ takes at least $n_v+1$ distinct values along the run, all on the grid.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{lane:rc-optimal}
$RC(k)$ is optimal among one-player stopping SSGs with no average vertex: there
$L\le|\Vmax|=N-2$, attained. A one-player family with $L>N-2$ must therefore
have $a\ge1$ and must switch some vertex more than once.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:linear-state}
$RC$, $ALH$ and $CL$ all improve on \Cref{fs14:lane-def}, whose $N$ is
$\Theta(k\log k)$ for the same run length $k$; $RC(k)$ is the extreme point,
$L=N-2$, and it is elementary (it is Howard's rule on a deterministic
shortest-path MDP and should be attributed as folklore). $CL(k)$ is the
cheapest lane with no tie along its run. None is superlinear, and by
\Cref{lane:autonomy} none can be made so by iteration: $\Vmax$ is autonomous in
each, so the whole game is a single module and no re-run is possible. Note that
a lane whose $k$ exit values are pairwise distinct needs $k-2$ average vertices
merely to hold those values, so $N\ge2k$: within \emph{that} sub-family $CL$ is
optimal, and the way $RC$ and $ALH$ beat it is precisely by making all the exit
values equal and living on the ties, which is legitimate because all-switches
keeps ties (and is why those two families are degenerate).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Binarisation of a multi-action state}

\begin{lemma}[A Max tree is an $\arg\max$ with logarithmic lag]\label{lane:tree}
Let $s$ be a state with $r\ge2$ actions and let $T_s$ be a rooted binary tree
of $r-1$ fresh Max vertices whose $r$ leaves are the actions of $s$ (each leaf
edge carrying that action's first passage law). If the values of the $r$
actions do not change during $d:=\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$ consecutive rounds of an
all-switches run, then at the end of those rounds the root of $T_s$ selects a
leaf of maximal value, and the value of the root equals $\max_i\val(A_i)$.
The cost is $r-1$ Max vertices and no average vertices.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the height. A vertex at height $1$ compares its two leaves and
after one round selects the larger. If every vertex at height $\le j$ selects
the maximum of its subtree after $j$ rounds, then a vertex $v$ at height $j+1$
sees, from round $j$ on, the two subtree maxima as its children's values, and
switches if the other is strictly larger; after one further round it selects
the larger of the two, i.e.\ the maximum of its subtree. Ties are kept, which
is harmless since either choice attains the maximum.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The lag is real]\label{lane:tree-lag}
Take $\mathrm{Lane}(3)$ with exits $\tfrac78,\tfrac34,\tfrac58$ and add
$u=\max(l_1,l_2)$, $p=\max(u,l_3)$; realised as an honest SSG this is $15$
vertices ($5$ Max, $8$ average, $2$ sinks), stopping, and the normal form is
verified from the graph. From the strategy ``all three lane vertices exit,
$u\mapsto l_1$, $p\mapsto u$'' the all-switches run is three rounds, and at
round $1$ the best leaf is worth $1$ while the root $p$ is worth $\tfrac78$:
the root is strictly behind. (\texttt{tree.py}; exact arithmetic.)
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What a binarisation of the published counters would need]
\label{lane:binarise}
From memory, unchecked against the sources. Fearnley (ICALP 2010) gives an MDP
on which Howard's rule takes $2^{\Omega(n)}$ iterations under the total- and
average-reward criteria; its bit state $b_i$ has $2i+O(1)$ actions (a
probabilistic self-loop $a_i$, the states $x_i,y_i$, and one action into each
of the $2i$ states of a deceleration lane), and each lane state has three
actions, so the instance has $\Theta(n^2)$ states and $\Theta(n^2)$ actions.
Friedmann (LMCS 2011) gives the analogous parity/mean-payoff/discounted/SSG
family, with $d_i$ of out-degree $2i+O(1)$ and $r,s$ of out-degree $n+1$.
Christ and Yannakakis (STOC 2023) do the same for reachability MDPs. Hansen
and Zwick (2010) give $\Omega(n^2)$ with $\Theta(n)$ actions. Melekopoglou and
Condon (1994) is the only two-action lower bound and it is for the
\emph{least-index} rule. Mukherjee and Kalyanakrishnan (ICAPS 2025) record that
for a constant number of actions per state the best known lower bound for
Howard's rule is linear.

Two of the three ingredients binarise at polynomial cost.
\emph{Selection}: \Cref{lane:tree} replaces an $r$-action state by $r-1$ binary
Max vertices, so Fearnley's $\Theta(n^2)$ actions become $\Theta(n^2)$ Max
vertices --- polynomial. \emph{Delay}: a chain of $d$ Max vertices, each with
its second action a constant, transmits a value change in exactly $d$ rounds
(\Cref{lane:three} is the extreme case), so a delay of $d$ rounds costs $d$
vertices, and Fearnley's total delay budget $\sum_i(2i+1)=\Theta(n^2)$ is
affordable. What does \emph{not} transfer is the \emph{timing}: by
\Cref{lane:tree} the selection at a state is correct only $\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$
rounds after its action values settle, and \Cref{lane:tree-lag} shows the root
is strictly behind while they move --- which in the counters they do, every
iteration, by design. The missing step is exactly this, and we state it as a
gap rather than pretend to it.

\textsc{Gap.} \emph{Is there a choice of binary selection trees and delay
chains for Fearnley's MDP, of total size $n^{O(1)}$, such that the all-switches
run of the resulting two-action instance reproduces the appeal ordering at
every bit state in every round --- equivalently, such that for every $i$ and
every round the root of $b_i$'s tree selects the same action that $b_i$ selects
in the source instance, up to a fixed per-state lag?}
\end{remark}

\subsection{Measurements}

\begin{proposition}[Measured maxima]\label{lane:measured}
All figures exact, all games one-player and stopping. Local search
(simulated annealing with exact evaluation) over harmonic normal forms with
$m$ Max vertices, every action reading at most three Max vertices, dyadic with
denominator $32$ or $64$, objective the bottom-antipodal height of the
improvement orientation (= the longest all-switches run over all $2^m$ starts):
the longest runs found were
\[
  m=4:\ 6,\qquad m=5:\ 8,\qquad m=6:\ 8,\qquad m=7:\ 8 .
\]
The value $6$ at $m=4$ is $h^\ast_{HK}(4)$, the ceiling of
\Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp}; the $m=5$ instance of height $8$ is
\emph{degenerate} ($2$ tied incidences over the cube, none along the run), so
it is not bound by that ceiling, and $8<h^\ast_{HK}(5)=11$ (measured,
unverified) $\le h^\ast(5)=12$. In that run one Max vertex switches four times
and a second switches four times. Local search at the level of the graph, over
one-player stopping SSGs with $n$ non-sinks, gave runs of length
$5,6,7,8,8,9$ at $n=5,\dots,10$, i.e.\ never more than $n=N-2$, which $RC(n)$
attains. This is a measurement over an engineered search space and proves
nothing; in particular no search in this project has ever found a hard
instance that was not first engineered.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[Where the route stands]\label{lane:verdict}
The construction the route was opened to build --- a lane re-used
$\omega(1)$ times --- is blocked, and the block is now a proof rather than a
failed search: \Cref{lane:impedance-cancels} refutes the premise (the escape
denominator amplifies the gap, not the rise), \Cref{lane:exit-chain} closes the
single-driver architecture, and \Cref{lane:autonomy} closes every architecture
in which the re-used module is self-contained. What is \emph{not} closed is a
lane driven by vertices that read the lane as a whole, since then no proper
subset is closed and \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never} is vacuous; the exact
scans reported in \Cref{lane:budget} found nothing there either, but they
covered $k\le5$ only.
\end{remark}

\begin{question}[Measured: nothing beats the reachability chain]\label{lane:nminus2}
Is $L\le N-2$ for every one-player stopping SSG? A local search whose objective
was exactly the length of the all-switches run, over one-player stopping SSGs
with $n=N-2$ non-sinks and every $(|\Vmax|,|\Vavg|)$ split, returned
$n=5,6,7,8,9,10\mapsto L=5,6,7,8,8,9$: never more than $n$, and the optimum
$L=n$ is $RC(n)$ of \Cref{lane:three}. At $a=0$ the bound is a theorem
(\Cref{lane:rc-optimal}); with $a$ held fixed the search returned $L=m$ exactly
--- $a=1$ with $m=3,\dots,7$ and $a=2$ with $m=3,\dots,6$ --- one short of
$N-2$ and far below the grid bound $m2^{a}$ of \Cref{lane:grid}, so the extra
randomness bought nothing at these sizes. This is a measurement over an
engineered search space and is offered as a question, not as evidence: a
one-player family with a superpolynomial run would in particular have to break
it, and every hard instance in this project had to be engineered rather than
found.
\end{question}
